entries.title: The Hijrah (622 CE)
entries.summary: The Hijrah — migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE — begins the Islamic calendar and transforms the Muslim community into a polity.
entries.detailed_information: See also the detailed Seerah entry on Hijrah. It is one of the most important chronological anchors in Islamic history.
entries.historical_significance: Epoch-making event for Islamic chronology and community formation.

entries.title: Mongol Sack of Baghdad (1258)
entries.summary: In 1258 CE Mongol forces under Hulagu Khan captured Baghdad, ending the classical Abbasid caliphate in Iraq.
entries.detailed_information: The conquest caused massive destruction according to classical reports. It is often treated as a symbolic end of an era, though Islamic civilization continued vigorously under other powers such as the Mamluks and later Ottomans.
entries.historical_significance: Major rupture in the political center of classical Sunni caliphate.
related_questions: Why did the Abbasid Caliphate decline?

entries.title: Recovery of Jerusalem (1187)
entries.summary: After Hattin, Salahuddin recovered Jerusalem in 1187 CE, a landmark event of the Crusades era.
entries.detailed_information: Jerusalem's change of hands carried immense religious symbolism for Muslims, Christians, and Jews. Classical Muslim sources emphasize relatively orderly transfer compared with the Crusader conquest of 1099, though modern historians analyze these narratives carefully.
entries.historical_significance: Central event in Crusades-era Islamic history.
